newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Pit bulls love you, really.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pit bulls love you, really.

text.p: Pit bulls are not mean, just misunderstood.

During the 1980s, pit bull attacks on people made headlines and the dogs were coveted by drug dealers and other underworld figures who bred them and trained them for duties such as guarding drug caches. But Marcia Curran and fellow pit bull owners say the much-maligned, much-feared terrier is a funny, loyal companion with an "infectious love of life."

Out of the Pits, an organisation that rescues abused and neglected pit bulls, brought Curran and about 40 others together at an Albany pet shop recently to celebrate "American Pit Bull Awareness Day" aimed at dispelling the dogs' killer image.

"The pit bull terriers are great animals, they get along with everyone at my house," said Curran, the mother of three children whose menagerie of pets also includes other dogs, cats, birds, goats, rabbits, chickens and guinea pigs.

She adopted a pit bull named Maggie from a woman who bought the dog from an unlicensed breeder who was trying to sell Maggie and two other pit bulls to drug dealers. Her other pit bull, "Reilly," was found starving and tied up with his mother and four siblings, three of whom died.
In their brochures, Out of the Pits members call pit bull terriers "the world's most misunderstood breed." But they say, "not very long ago, it was America's favourite dog."
"Although this is a high energy dog that requires a very firm hand, it possesses an infectious love of life. Properly trained, it is comical, loving and loyal to a fault," the brochure says.

Some famous pit bull terriers were RCA Victor's "Nipper," Buster Brown's pal "Tige," who lived in a shoe, and the Little Rascals' "Petey" -- just three examples of the thousands of pit bulls trusted with America's young.

The breed descended from England's Staffordshire Terrier, a devoted family dog known as the "children's nursemaid." In the Middle Ages its ancestors were bred to bait bears and bulls for public amusement, which was eventually outlawed in England. They were then cross-bred with terriers and thrown into pits to fight.
Out of the Pits, whose slogan is "help us get them into your hearts," seeks to make the public aware of the gentle nature of the American Pit Bull Terrier and American Staffordshire Terrier.

"Drug dealers illegally breed pit bulls to be man-aggressive by torturing them," Mary Allen, the organisation's co-director, said. "By the end of the '80s the pit bull had become the underworld's macho dog."
The group's own mascot, "Raymon," was rescued from drug dealers and is taken into schools to help teach children about the joys of owning a pitbull.

"They put staples in their feet and bottle caps under their skin to make them vicious, pump them up with steroids for use as fighters, take out their voice boxes with home surgery so they will guard the drugs without making a sound," Allen said of some of the hardships endured by the dogs at the hands of dealers.
"The people that should have them are afraid of them and the people who shouldn't have them, have them," Cydney Cross, another group co-director, said.
When they were used for dog fighting, many of the animals were left to die -- abandoned at veterinarians' offices or thrown into rivers or trash bins.
The pit bull group uses a post office box address because it fears the dogs will be stolen if anyone knows where they are kept before they are sent to animal shelters, Cross said.
